 WATCH: Coach Jans Press Conference - 11/19/26
 November 19, 2026 | Men's Basketball
 Share: STARKVILLE - Mississippi State head coach Chris Jans met with the media leading into Friday's matchup in Jackson, Miss. against Tulsa
 2026-27 Mississippi State Men's Basketball Quotes 
 Coach Jans Media Session – November 19, 2026 
 Transcript Powered by State 1878 
 State Head Coach Chris Jans 
 Opening Statement 
 CJ: "I'd like to personally give my condolences to Jerine Bierie and the Bob Bierie family back in Dubuque, Iowa. Coach Bob Bierie was a young mentor of mine. He was the football coach/athletic director at my alma mater, Loras College, and I've known him since I was 17 years old. I didn't play for him nor did I work for him, but he had a huge impact on my life from the time I met him till this summer when my wife and I, Sheri, were able to spend a few hours with him and his wife, as he battled of an illness for some quite some time, and he passed a couple days ago. He meant a lot to the Dubuque community and to Loras college community. He's someone that was very, very, very well respected and loved, and he's certainly going to be missed."
"On a positive note, I'd like to congratulate Coach OB [Kevin O'Brien] and the women's soccer team, the year that they're having, certainly getting to host an NCAA tournament game at home is quite the thrill. Then Julie Darty Dennis and the volleyball team heading into the SEC tournament. I want to wish them both well and good luck, and I'll open up to questions."
 Q: Can you talk about Josh Hubbard and Kimani Hamilton played back home in Jackson? 
 CJ: "I guess Kimani's a lucky benefactor. This was more for two reasons. As you know, we've spread this game around and I love doing it. We have played in Southaven/Memphis, Tupelo, and Jackson since we've been here. It's important to me to try to do that and try to get to different corners of the state and kind of bring the game to some of our Bulldog fans. The ones that do travel, make it easier for them occasionally. But when we scheduled this game, and certainly, as you know, we do this in advance, it was for two reasons. One I just stated, but also with Josh being a senior I thought this would be kind of cool for him to be able to play in his hometown in his senior season. With the landscape changing and the five for five being in place, who knows if this will be his last time playing in that area of the country."
"I'd imagine they're excited. The great thing for me as a coach is you're always worried about distractions, and with their personalities, the way they carry themselves, it won't affect their play. So, it's awesome that we're able to do that, and certainly honoring Josh with this 2,000-point deal and being able to do it in front of his hometown and more family and friends than maybe normal, is quite the treat as well."
 Q: What does playing in Jackson, Miss. mean to Josh and Kimani? 
 CJ: "I'd imagine on a personal level it's pretty cool. It hearkens me back to when I got the job and all I heard about was Josh Hubbard when I got the job. I didn't know Josh Hubbard when I was coaching at New Mexico State. One of the first orders of business for myself and Coach [David] Anwar was to drive down to that area and meet the family and Josh and start the recruiting process for him."
"At the same time Kimani Hamilton was a young man that had signed with the program prior to my arrival. He's a year older than Josh, and I also made a trip down there to spend time with Kimani and his family. I still remember the conversation and how it went. With Tang being his father and being such a great player, I think it's a cool story that he's back here starting for the Bulldogs where he grew up wanting to play for, like his dad did. It's quite a circle that's brought him back here. I'd imagine they both've got a little extra bounce in their step heading into practice this afternoon before we bus on down there and get ready to play tomorrow night."
 Q: What are thoughts about Tulsa? 
 CJ: "Tulsa is led by Eric Konkol, who I've known for a long time. A very respected coach in our industry for being a good teacher, for running great programs, for being well prepared. They're a team that I'm familiar with, a coach I'm familiar with, and they don't beat themselves. They're very well prepared. They'll have a great game plan. They're going to try to take away our weaknesses, they're going to target certain players. They run their offense with great pace, and they know what they're trying to do. They're coming off a great season where they broke records. They won 30 games and finished in the finals of the NIT tournament."
"They've got great momentum this year. They are undefeated, 4-0. For me, like always, one of the challenges is to make sure our guys understand coming off a great, exhilarating road win against the Power 5 team, now we have to play a team that's not in the Power 5. Certainly, as coaches, it's not a lack of respect at all and we'll prepare just as hard as we did for that game as we are for this one, but sometimes young people can get it mixed up in their brain about who they're playing and maybe not prepare quite as well or hard or look at them differently. That'll be part of the challenge, and certainly we've already begun trying to do that."
 Q: How do you help teach Tristan Reed to prevent him from entering foul trouble? 
 CJ: "It's not just Tristan. Certainly, he's a big part of it. I think our team, in general, is fouling too much. Our free throw rate defensively is poor. I want to have an aggressive style of play, but that's always a fine line and I think it's a couple different reasons why. One, I think officials call the games closer at the beginning of the year, tighter. I thought the officials the other night was very consistent. They called a tight game. It didn't feel like an SEC game. Those guys are high level officials, all three of them. But they were very consistent with how they called the game, and we didn't adjust to it as players, as coaches, as well as we would have liked looking back."
"We've just got to be more disciplined. We've got what we try to use around our program is to trust the technique of how we guard the ball and where to position our hands and our feet. In close out techniques or at the rim plays where shielding has been very popular, it's something we work on every single day. A lot of different things, a lot of different techniques and getting those guys to buy into the techniques that we're trying to install since they've arrived in June, and a lot of them are doing it, but now they're not transferring it to live play and that's what's most important. We're going to continue to harp on them and try to devise new drills and new ways, certainly film and learning from our mistakes is big."
"Specifically, to Tristan, he's a valuable part of this year's team. I don't care how old he is. I don't care what is beside Tristan Reed , #33, what initials are there. He's got to have a big impact for us, and he did Tuesday. We've been waiting for it, and he's got to do it every single night, and he can't do it when he's saddled with foul problems. I think he's got all the tools to be an excellent defender. He's got length. He's a great kid. He plays hard, he's bouncy, he's got girth, he's got feel. He's just got to continue to trust the techniques and not put himself in harm's way."
 Q: What did you learn about depth of this team as enter foul trouble? 
 CJ: "I think being able to play 11 and even 12 guys one game, those first three games of the season was huge that way, not just giving everyone tape and minutes for us and for them individually but also giving them some confidence and giving us some confidence that we can handle a foul situation, knock on wood, because it's going to happen. It ain't the first time we're going to have people saddled with fouls, and then it allows you to make decisions. Are you going to play certain players with two in the 1st half, which is becoming more in vogue than maybe it was in the old school yesteryear."
"I think playing those games the way we did and having some opportunities to play guys, even in the Xavier game. You know, playing Jalyn Collingwood and Willie Burnett III a ton of minutes down the stretch to get them more prepared for future games, even though it was in a losing cause, hopefully it'll help us going forward that way."
 Q: Can you talk about the 2027 high school signed class? 
 CJ: "We signed four high school guys. Jacques Mitchell is a lightning-fast point guard from Tulsa, Oklahoma. He was the first verbal commit we had and I haven't coached him yet, but I think once we get our eyes on him and our hands on him, he'll be the fastest point guard that I've ever coached with the ball. At least that's our expectation that way. He's got a lot of ability, and guys that are built like that usually don't shoot the ball very well, but he shoots it pretty good walking in the door, so we're certainly excited about him."
"Jalen White is a wing from the Vegas area that plays at Bella Vista, which is a very respected program in the Phoenix area. Plays for a guy that's had great players in Mike George and Jalen is a dynamic player. He's got huge upside. He's got great length, great physical ability. He's a big-time jumper. He can make shots. His best basketball is definitely ahead of him and he's also a wonderful kid. We're excited about all four of them or we wouldn't have signed them."
"Chris Brown, ironically, plays in Phoenix as well but he is originally from the Bahamas, and in a positive way for us, his size and length is very unique. He's 6'9", but he's got like a 7'7" wingspan, which is freakish that way, and for us that's a big deal. The wingspans and the lengths and the reach are more important than how tall they are. How long their neck is or their torso is, in my opinion, doesn't help on the basketball court as much as the length of their limbs, if you will, helps them on the court. He's got great IQ. He knows how to play. He's got a good skill level. I think he has a chance to walk in and because of the length, because of the skill level, because of the feel, to impact us that way."
"The most recent one, Brisun Hammermeister, is a Florida kid from the Fort Myers area that caught her eye this summer. He was a little under the radar because of some injuries and moving around, but he's a hard playing guy and another wing that can move around. The last two years we've really tried to recruit guys that are more positionless and can play multiple positions, and Brisun can really shoot the ball. He kind of shoots it like Willie does, kind of behind his head a little bit that way, which makes it harder to get to, to contest, and he can get his shot off against pretty much anybody that way. He's a really, really hard playing kid."
"The theme for us in our last two classes have been just guys that are quality human beings, guys that possess the right mindset in terms of being about the right stuff, in our opinion, of working hard, having the right approach every single day from the diligence that we've done. We're certainly excited about the three freshmen that we had this year, and we're as excited as you can be about not coaching a group of young people of what we think they are on paper as well."
 Q: What was your reaction to King Grace shooting 14-14 from the free-throw line? 
 CJ: "You'd have to ask him about what he's working on when I'm not around. I know what we do when we're around and we're legally allowed to be with him and work on his game. I think more importantly in that game, it's like anything. It becomes contagious. When you start making it the rim gets bigger for us down the stretch to run a play for him to either get fouled or score when the game was in the balance, and then do it again on a side out situation, when it was really, really crucial as the game clock was, I think at 12. It speaks to our confidence that we had in him that particular night."
"I can't imagine that his confidence isn't through the roof right now. He made a huge three right in front of our bench that R.J. [Johnson] and [ Josh Hubbard ] set up for him with the dribble penetration that they both had leading up to the catch and shoot opportunity that King benefited from. He's in a really good place. He's playing very, very well. King's hard to guard. He's unpredictable a little bit, which can be frustrating as the coach, but playing against that is probably no fun. You don't know exactly what he's going to do at times, and he's full throttle. He's playing head down, and obviously, as a coach you get a little nervous sometimes, but in that particular game, it was really, Related News
